1) there was a marked variation between individual heifer growth rates; 2) heifer growth rate in the first 6 months of life is associated with the likelihood of reaching target service weight; 3) heifers whose growth rates in the first 3 months were below average were less likely to reach target service weight; and 4) the system used for measuring and recording heifer growth rates can be used by farmers to benchmark heifer growth rates on their own and on other

the growth rate of dairy heifers in the first 30 days after birth is very slow (median 0·12 kg/day) and is associated with lower heifer growth rate up to first service (420 days) and a lower probability of achieving target service weight (median 374 kg) by that time.
heifer growth rate up to weaning and to service age is a useful predictor of subsequent reproductive performance.

the data collected in this study can be used to benchmark heifer growth rates on UK dairy farms and that the system used is suitable for use on commercial farms.
the growth of heifers from birth to 180 days of age is important to future productivity and that growth rate is a useful indicator of the health and welfare of the animal.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the heifer growth monitoring system developed by AHDB Dairy and the Royal Veterinary College is a useful tool for dairy farmers to improve the growth and health of their heifers.
heifer growth rates in the UK are low and there is considerable potential for improvement, both for the individual heifer and for the whole dairy herd.

it is possible to collect heifer weights from birth to first service using a simple and cost-effective system, to monitor growth rates and feed-back to farmers.
the growth rate of heifers is a key determinant of their future performance.
